summary:
LUMEN is a prototype for evaluating lunar landing sites through sunlight and direct-to-Earth visibility. We built a Python calculation engine that combines NASA LRO/LOLA elevation models with JPL/NAIF SPICE ephemerides to estimate the terrain horizon and the positions of the Sun and Earth. It calculates visibility metrics, explores nearby candidate points, and generates regional maps. A web interface provides the foundation for interactive exploration. We tested the geometry with synthetic terrain and compared ephemerides against JPL Horizons. LUMEN brings terrain and orbital geometry into one workflow so teams can study how location and timing affect power and communications near the lunar south pole.

https://github.com/PabloVS044/lumen
details:
LUMEN examines how lunar terrain changes access to sunlight and direct communication with Earth. Its engine reads NASA LOLA elevation models at different resolutions and traces the horizon around a selected site, accounting for the Moon’s curvature. JPL/NAIF SPICE data provides the apparent positions of the Sun and Earth; the engine uses those positions and the horizon to calculate visibility and mission-relevant metrics. A nearby-site search filters candidate points by slope and evaluates promising locations. The prototype also produces regional map files and estimates horizon uncertainty from alternative terrain models.

We developed the engine with Python, NumPy, Rasterio, PyProj, SciPy and SpiceyPy. The web interface uses Next.js, React and TypeScript, with Protobuf and ConnectRPC contracts between components. Synthetic terrain tests check the horizon geometry, and JPL Horizons provides an independent ephemeris comparison. The interactive visualizations and the complete web analysis flow are still being integrated.
